À Parc-Extension, le BBQ sans frontières: In Parc-Extension, the BBQ sans frontières turns a free feast into a manifesto for inclusion and migrant justice.
L’affiche du festival à l’entrée du Parc: The festival poster at the entrance to Parc Dickie-Moore. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
On dit souvent que la cuisine est le cœu: They often say food is the heart of a culture. Here at the BBQ sans frontières, it was as if food had become the heart of a struggle. Around the tables, I saw stories cross paths and heard all kinds of journeys. It let me understand, on the ground, how the fight to help migrants is organized and how it breaks down borders.
Le combat d’un réfugié sud-asiatique n’e: The struggle of a South Asian refugee is not the same as that of an African or a South American. But their needs, their hardships, their fights end up coming together. One word kept coming back: dignity. And right after it: mutual aid.
Briser les frontières, oui. Au sens figu: Breaking down borders, yes. In the figurative sense: breaking down the borders that policies, fear-driven rhetoric and exclusion impose. But also the intimate borders, the ones we sometimes carry in our heads, that separate communities from one another. That day, at the BBQ sans frontières, it all blended together: the smells, the languages, the stories – and that’s what I’m sharing with you in this article.
Dimanche 14 septembre, midi. Le soleil e: Sunday, September 14, noon. The sun is at its peak, warming the air, while a festive breeze moves through Parc Dickie-Moore in Parc-Extension, Montréal. In this 4,000-square-metre green space, the BBQ sans frontières is under way, the first street food festival organized by the Super Boat People collective. While the event is meant to delight the taste buds, it is above all a community manifesto: a response to the exclusion and invisible walls that certain federal policies put up against migrants and asylum seekers.
Une heure seulement après l’ouverture, l: Only an hour after opening, the park is overflowing with life. The air is thick with the smell of grilled food, music and the voices of festivalgoers. Lines grow longer in front of the booths, colourful plates of food from here and elsewhere pass from hand to hand, and children zigzag between the tables and benches set up for the occasion.
<strong>Le cœur à la fête, la tête au po: Hearts set on celebration, minds on politics
Assise à un kiosque pour enfants, Audrey: Seated at a kids’ booth, Audrey-Anne Paquette draws with her son Arthur. They live in the neighbourhood and didn’t hesitate to cross the street when they saw the festival announcement. “It feels good to have a positive space where we gather around values of welcome, inclusion and migrant justice,” the mother explains. Arthur, pencil in hand, cuts in: “It’s cool because it’s open to everyone. You can draw, eat and, on top of that, the food is free!”
Au-delà de la fête, Audrey-Anne confie ê: Beyond the party, Audrey-Anne says she came to support migrants. “The super harsh, discriminatory policies toward asylum seekers worry me a lot,” she says, referring to Bill C-2, titled the “Strong Borders Act,” currently being debated in Ottawa.
Présenté par le gouvernement fédéral com: Presented by the federal government as a measure to “secure the borders” and “better regulate immigration,” the bill introduces significant restrictions on political asylum, strengthens the state’s surveillance powers and tightens the criteria for recognizing refugee status. But this Sunday in Parc-Ex, the Super Boat People collective’s initiative opens tables rather than closing doors, and this look at current events also connects to an older memory, one embedded at the heart of the organizing collective.
« Beaucoup d’entre nous ont des parents: “Many of us have parents or grandparents who fled their country. We see ourselves in the Boat People,” says Eddy, a young man originally from Congo, before slipping away, too shy, he says, to continue the conversation.
Son témoignage, bref mais chargé de sens: His brief but meaningful statement sums up the spirit of the Super Boat People collective. Created by the children and grandchildren of Southeast Asian refugees, it takes its name from the thousands of men and women who took to the sea in the 1970s to flee repression. Welcomed in Canada, they built communities that are now rooted in Montréal. Fifty years later, their descendants celebrate that legacy by opening it up to other migration journeys – from Africa, Latin America and the Middle East.
« C’est le 50<sup>e</sup> anniversaire d: “This year is the 50<sup>th</sup> anniversary of the arrival of Southeast Asian refugees in Montréal. Most people in the collective, their grandparents or parents, are refugees, and they’ve been here for 50 years,” says the organizing team, which includes Rémy Chhem, Marie-Ève Samson and Maya Tran. For them, this festival is both a celebration and a stand: “It’s also a way of showing solidarity with contemporary struggles, with the issues facing immigrants and refugees today. [...] It’s important to show solidarity with migrant groups who arrived more recently and to fight for their rights, which have been in decline since we got here.”
À Parc-Ex, ce dimanche, la mémoire se co: In Parc-Ex this Sunday, memory is thus joined with the present: around the tables, generations and journeys intersect. Borders fade, differences become riches, and sharing a meal turns into a unifying political gesture.
À l’entrée du parc, ce sont d’abord les: At the park entrance, it is first the booths of community organizations that greet visitors. It’s a route that recalls the often-overlooked priorities of migrants: before even sharing a meal, the point is to remind people that basic needs – finding housing, learning French, feeding one’s family – are still far from guaranteed. Afrique au féminin, the only women’s centre in Parc-Extension, is one of them.
Depuis 40 ans, l’organisme accompagne le: For 40 years, the organization has supported immigrant women in their integration. Its presence at the festival is a chance to shed light on realities that often go unspoken and to make its services known: French classes, a drop-in daycare, creative workshops and food assistance. “Every Tuesday, we distribute about 300 food baskets,” says Élisabeth Atchadé, coordinator of the PAM project and mobilization officer for Afrique au féminin. “There’s a need as basic as eating in the neighbourhood,” she insists. “Here, our strength is collaboration,” Élisabeth continues.
Élisabeth Atchadé, d’Afrique au féminin,: Élisabeth Atchadé, of Afrique au féminin, in front of the organization’s booth. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Après les services et l’entraide viennen: After the services and mutual aid come the food stalls, and finally the main stage. On it, the masters of ceremonies, including Jimmy Ung, a member of the Super Boat People board of directors, invite audience members to recognize one another. “Who here is an immigrant or the parent of an immigrant?” the hosts ask the crowd. Glances are exchanged, some people nod, others raise a hand. “Say hi to your neighbour!” The park rings with bursts of laughter and with shy or knowing greetings.
Ce moment de connivence prépare le terra: This moment of complicity sets the stage for the day’s activities. “We have something exciting to tell you. First, we’re going to educate ourselves, and then we’ll celebrate,” they announce, alluding to the workshops and talks to come. A moment of education to immerse the audience in the history of migration, to understand the rights of asylum seekers and to reflect collectively on current challenges. On the program: a workshop organized with Brique par brique on housing in Parc-Extension, and a discussion with the Observatoire pour la justice migrante and the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes.
Arrivée du Brésil il y a six ans, Débora: Déborah, who arrived from Brazil six years ago, says she was quickly drawn to the festival’s concept, which promotes mutual aid but also shares information with migrants and asylum seekers: “It’s important to see how people organize to help their community and others.” Beside her, Nancy, a Montrealer born to Ivorian and Congolese parents, agrees. “I like the idea of bringing several communities together […] Communities often meet around food. I think it’s a great way to show what immigration contributes. It has to be recognized!” she says.
L’accessibilité est à la base du festiva: Accessibility is the foundation of the festival. Everything is offered, from refreshing drinks to the whole range of dishes served. On site: Filipino, pan-African, Lebanese, Indian and Mexican cuisine. And for the occasion, there are plenty of restaurateurs who chose to give their time, know-how and recipes without counting.
Pour Rémy Chhem, cofondateur de Super Bo: For Rémy Chhem, cofounder of Super Boat People, this free access is central: “When was the first time, or the last time, you saw a free street food festival with eight chefs, including professionals who have their own restaurants?” he calls out to the festivalgoers.
Puis, il en vient à l’essentiel : « Un b: Then he gets to the heart of it: “A barbecue, what does that mean? It’s people coming together, it’s cultures meeting, it’s people trying new things, getting to know one another.”
Et la gratuité n’exclut pas la solidarit: And free doesn’t rule out solidarity: everyone is invited to contribute according to their means. Rémy Chhem says the voluntary contributions and donations collected will be used wisely: “All the proceeds will go to an immigration organization chosen by the chefs. We hope to raise a few thousand dollars to support work that is really urgent right now.”
Cette approche se retrouve dans l’engage: This approach is reflected in the chefs’ commitment. For several hours now, the lines at the food stands haven’t gotten any shorter. With a colourful scarf on her head, Carla, the chef at the restaurant Piel Canela, makes sure all her pots are full before the next wave of customers. On her plates, shredded halal chicken “so that all communities can eat” – alongside esquite (grilled corn) and a salad of cactus (nopales) and frijoles – served with a taco.
Carla, cheffe du restaurant Piel Canela,: Carla, chef at the restaurant Piel Canela, behind her stand. Photo credit: Nantou Soumahoro
Offrir gratuitement ses plats allait de: Offering her dishes for free was a given for the chef, who says she was the first to respond favourably to Super Boat People’s proposal. “I find this initiative so brilliant. It’s in line with my values. I work with cooks who are migrants. Several members of my team are asylum seekers.” She has lived in Canada for 14 years and says her own arrival went well, but that the road is much harder for others. “So if I can do something to help, I will.”
Les festivaliers accueillent cette génér: Festivalgoers welcome this generosity with enthusiasm, aware of how lucky they are to have access to varied, quality food without having to open their wallets.
« En général, ce genre de nourriture est: “Generally, this kind of food is very expensive,” observes Cassandra, who came to the festival with her two children. “Here, we can taste dishes we wouldn’t necessarily be able to afford.” For her, this accessibility is a breath of fresh air: “Seriously, people love it. There are lots of activities, mostly free, so for every budget. And the kids get to discover different kinds of cultures.”
Au-delà des plats partagés, Cassandra vo: Beyond the shared dishes, Cassandra sees the event as an antidote to the prevailing narrative about migrants and asylum seekers: “On the news, you often see the negative side. But here, we discover the positive side of people who have integrated and want to share their culture.”
Au cours de la fête, les représentants d: During the festivities, representatives of the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes (TCRI) take the mic to remind everyone that solidarity also means defending rights.
Leur message s’appuie sur une déclaratio: Their message draws on a declaration prepared over more than a year with their members, which sets out five principles: social justice, legacy and transmission to future generations, respect for dignity and human rights, collective and shared responsibility, and living together.
« On voulait envoyer un message très for: “We wanted to send a very strong message to the government: welcome must be extended with dignity,” stresses François Loza-Rodriguez, analysis and advocacy coordinator for the organization, which has 158 members across Quebec.
« Quand les immigrants et les réfugiés a: “When immigrants and refugees arrive here, sometimes they don’t have the same rights or the same services as Quebec citizens. […] Yet these people have gone through a whole migration journey, which can be very complex, very difficult,” he says.
La TCRI n’a pas voulu en rester aux mots: The TCRI did not want to stop at words: its declaration also took the form of a rap workshop with two Montréal artists, Kama and Nawfal, a way of giving these principles a popular, unifying resonance.
« Aujourd’hui, on entend beaucoup de dis: “Today, we hear a lot of polarizing, negative rhetoric against immigrants and refugees. What we want to put forward is solidarity, inclusion, dignity,” says François.
Sur scène, les maîtres de cérémonie rapp: On stage, the masters of ceremonies point out that the celebration takes place in a rather heavy context. “Vulnerable communities are increasingly marginalized because of a lack of access to affordable housing and restrictive immigration policies, like the new Bill C-2,” they list. At the mention of the bill, the crowd reacts: “Boo!” several voices shout, taken up in chorus. A thunder of disapproval rises from the audience, turning the moment into a collective reminder that, behind the shared plates, the struggles are still burning.
Déposé au printemps 2025, le projet de l: Tabled in spring 2025, Bill C-2 provides, among other things, for shortening the deadlines to file an asylum claim, tightening the criteria for obtaining refugee status and expanding the powers of the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) with respect to detention and removal.
Des organismes de défense des droits ale: Rights advocacy organizations warn that C-2 weakens both the right to asylum, protected by the 1951 Geneva Convention, and privacy and procedural fairness for the entire Canadian population. Adopted in the aftermath of the Second World War, the 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees is the cornerstone of international asylum law. It recognizes the right of anyone persecuted because of their race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinions to seek protection in another country. Its fundamental principle – non-refoulement – prohibits sending a refugee back to a territory where their life or freedom would be threatened. By acceding to it in 1969, Canada committed to guaranteeing a fair, individual examination of each asylum claim, without discrimination or arbitrary obstacles.
Le projet de loi C-2 fait face à de vive: Bill C-2 has faced sharp criticism since it was tabled in June, because several of its provisions appear to contradict these international commitments. By limiting access to the asylum process for people who have transited through a “safe third country,” shortening the deadlines to file a claim and restricting avenues of appeal, Ottawa is creating obstacles that undermine the fundamental right to seek asylum. Moreover, the expansion of the Border Services Agency’s detention and removal powers increases the risk of a person being sent back to a country where they could face persecution. These are all measures that organizations such as Amnesty International and the Canadian Council for Refugees consider incompatible with the spirit of the Geneva Convention.
Et la mobilisation est large : plus de 3: And the mobilization is broad: more than 300 organizations across the country, including unions, legal associations, community groups and migrant rights organizations, have called for the bill to be withdrawn. In Quebec, organizations such as the Observatoire pour la justice migrante, which was present for a workshop on the day of the festival, also denounce the bill. “This is a bill that is dangerous for migrants,” explains Amel Zaazaa, the organization’s cofounder and director. “If there’s one thing civil society is unanimous about right now, it’s that this bill really must be withdrawn,” she insists.
M<sup>me</sup> Zaazaa souligne que les l: Ms.<sup></sup> Zaazaa points out that current struggles give organizations and community groups a chance to step out of their silos and come together. “It opens up shared spaces for us, where our fights meet and converge.”

Pour que ces organisations puissent fair: So that these organizations can make their voices heard, the response will take to the streets: on September 20, the nationwide mobilization Fixons les limites, or Draw the Line. The Montréal leg will be held at Parc Jeanne-Mance. Ms. Zaazaa describes the demonstration as “a beautiful convergence of struggles around migrant justice, justice for Indigenous peoples and ecological justice.” Then, on October 19, the group Solidarité sans frontières is inviting migrants, undocumented people or those at risk of becoming undocumented, along with their allies, to gather at Parc metro station in Montréal to demand regularization for people without status.
Au-delà d’une fête de quartier, le BBQ s: More than a neighbourhood party, the BBQ sans frontières is a starting point, a call to continue the fight well beyond this festive day.
